 How does daylight saving time impact drivers?
 By Steve Karesh 
 November 6, 2026 | 
 7:42 PM 
 | 
 One of the biggest risks associated with daylight saving time is on the roads — not in our schedules or in our beds.
 The public and government affairs manager for AAA in the D.C. region, Ragina Ali, told WTOP that there are risks to the public associated with changing the clocks.
 “I can tell you that fatal crashes involving pedestrians and bicyclists increase roughly by about 13% in the five weeks after the fall time change,” Ali said. “Largely due to darker evening commutes and poor visibility by motorists to see pedestrians and bicyclists.”
 Adding to the danger on the roads is wildlife, Ali said. Car crashes involving animals such as deer rise by about 6% in the first four weeks after time falls back, with a sharper spike in nighttime wildlife collisions.
 Dr. Scott Schecter, pulmonary and critical care physician at U.Va. Health, said that time change can “upset your underlying schedule,” and that it often takes several days for even a healthy person’s body to adjust. If there are underlying psychiatric conditions or health problems, it can take even longer.
 For those who are sensitive toward time shifts, Schecter recommends adjusting your schedule in small increments even before you set your clocks back.
 Along with the decrease in visibility due to the earlier sunrise, drivers may be more drowsy immediately following the time change, which would also make them more prone to accidents. 
 Ali said that the “AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety has conducted research that would show that drowsy driving was probably a factor in about 18% of traffic fatalities between 2017 and 2021.”
 Drowsiness behind the wheel is of concern to Schecter as well. He said that being sleepy behind the wheel could be a sign of a more serious problem.
 “If you’re doing something like driving or talking to someone and you can’t stay awake during that, I think those would be concerning symptoms.”
 According to the Metropolitan Washington Council of Governments, earlier sunsets each fall create a well-documented spike in pedestrian and cyclist crashes.
 “As darkness falls during peak travel hours, drivers, pedestrians, and bicyclists face increased dangers on regional roadways,” the Metropolitan Washington Council of Governments said. 
 The council’s executive director, Clark Mercer, held a news conference in Silver Spring, Maryland, Thursday, addressing pedestrian and cyclist safety during its Street Smart campaign.
 Mercer said there are nearly 4,000 pedestrian and bicycle crashes in the D.C. metro region each year and there are three things local governments must do to bring that number down.
 “Educate folks to make sure that they are being mindful on the roads, especially during this period of the year, with daylight savings time, we have to engineer our streets so that these cars cannot go at such high rates of speed, so that they go the speed limit or slower. And we have to enforce the laws,” Mercer said.
 A recent study has found that in the U.S., fatal crashes among motor-vehicle occupants decreased in the five weeks after the fall time change (-7.1%), while fatal crashes among pedestrians/bicyclists increased during the same period (+13%). The inverse was true after the springtime change.
